progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From b01: homeostasis, tolerance range and set point; the five parts; negative feedback opposes a change and eases as the variable returns; the hypothalamus as a control centre (temperature). From Year 11: osmosis (water moves across a partially permeable membrane towards the side with more dissolved particles); membranes contain channel proteins; hormones travel in the blood to target cells with receptors; neurons carry nerve impulses. Not assumed: osmolarity, nephron, filtrate, reabsorption, collecting duct, osmoreceptor, posterior pituitary, ADH, aquaporin, diuresis, aldosterone.
progression.startsWith: Connect blood osmolarity to ADH and nephron permeability. The video opens: On a hot day when you haven't had much to drink, you pass a small amount of dark yellow urine.
progression.stopsAfter: naming blood osmolarity (the concentration of dissolved particles) as the regulated variable, not the volume drunk; describing filtration and reabsorption in a nephron, with the collecting duct setting the final water kept; tracing a rise in osmolarity through osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus (which shrink as water leaves them), nerve impulses to the posterior pituitary (neural) and ADH in the blood (hormonal; made in the hypothalamus, released from the pituitary), with thirst replacing water the kidney can only conserve; explaining how ADH inserts aquaporins into the collecting duct so water leaves by osmosis into the concentrated surrounding tissue, giving a small volume of concentrated urine; explaining the loop as negative feedback and running it in reverse after drinking water (less ADH, fewer aquaporins, a large volume of dilute urine); contrasting aldosterone (low blood volume or pressure, more sodium reabsorbed, water follows by osmosis); predicting ADH and urine changes for a salty snack and interpreting urine output after water against a salt solution of blood concentration.
progression.nextLesson: how plants keep enough water (route entry bio-m8-b05).

teaching.task: On a hot day with little to drink, you pass a small amount of dark urine. Drink a litre of water quickly, and within an hour or so you pass a lot of pale urine. What tells your kidneys how much water to keep, and how do they do it?
teaching.causalExplanation: Causes: why losing water raises osmolarity (same particles, less water; 2); why the collecting duct matters (it sets the last of the water kept; 3); how the receptor detects (it shrinks by osmosis; 4); why water leaves the duct (aquaporins plus a concentrated surrounding tissue; 5); why the loop eases (osmoreceptors swell back; 6); why aldosterone moves water at all (water follows sodium by osmosis; 8). Attention: everyday urine colour (1), the 180 L against 1.5 L surprise (3). Visual medium: a gauge that slides with every change, matched pairs for the receptor and the duct, and the two sample cups as the output. Apply: predict for a salt load (10a), interpret a two-line graph (10c). Remember: "anti-wee" and "water follows salt".
teaching.conversationalApproach: On a hot day with little to drink you pass a small amount of dark urine, and after a litre of water you pass a lot of pale urine, so the question is what tells your kidneys how much water to keep and how they do it. The regulated variable is not how much you drink but blood osmolarity, how much dissolved salt and other particles are in each litre of plasma, with Year 11 osmosis as the rule behind the whole video. The kidneys filter about a hundred and eighty litres a day yet you pass about one and a half, because most of the filtrate is reabsorbed and the collecting duct sets how much of the rest you keep. Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus shrink slightly when blood is too concentrated, the hypothalamus signals by nerve impulses to the posterior pituitary, which releases ADH, and thirst is the drinking side. ADH moves aquaporins into the duct membrane so water leaves the duct by osmosis into the concentrated tissue around it, giving a small volume of concentrated urine; as osmolarity falls the osmoreceptors swell back and ADH falls, which is negative feedback. The litre of water runs the same loop in reverse. Aldosterone is the contrast: it responds mainly to low blood volume or pressure and increases sodium reabsorption, and water follows the salt. The memory aid is ADH the anti-wee hormone and, for aldosterone, water follows salt, then two exam questions with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: On a hot day when you haven't had much to drink, you pass a small amount of dark yellow urine. Drink a litre of water quickly, and within an hour or so you pass a lot of pale urine. Same kidneys, same day, opposite results. The colour is a clue: similar wastes dissolved in less water, or in more. So what tells your kidneys how much water to keep, and how do they do it?
teaching.understandingCheck: 10a is a predict and explain item (the route's stop: changed intake, here salt without water). 10c is an interpret item from a two-line graph (changed intake: water against a salt solution of blood concentration). Each ends "Pause here to answer." with a 10 s countdown; the whole card stays on screen during the countdown and after it. Feedback is brief (about 25 to 30 s): the answer, the key reasons, givens underlined in the card as they are used, one crossed-out classic mistake. No givens card.
teaching.curriculumScope: B8-IQ1-02 (p 56): "investigate the various mechanisms used by organisms to maintain their internal environment within tolerance limits, including:" with the listed example "internal coordination systems that allow homeostasis to be maintained, including hormones and neural pathways (ACSBL112, ACSBL113, ACSBL114)". The neural step (hypothalamus to posterior pituitary by nerve impulses) and the hormonal step (ADH in the blood) are both named in scene 4; aldosterone is a second hormone on the same organ (scene 8). "Within tolerance limits" is carried by osmolarity's range (scene 2) and the loop (scene 6).

design.visualSystem: A concentration gauge owns the upper right from scene 2: a coded horizontal bar labelled "blood osmolarity" with a pale band "normal range" in the middle and a marker that slides right ("more concentrated") or left ("more dilute") as the story changes; the urine sample cups sit beneath it when urine is the output. The working area at the left and centre holds one painted plate or one matched pair at a time with callouts. b01's loop ring fills in scene 6 and returns as a thumbnail in 7, 10b and 11. Water molecules are small coded blue dots (abstract), salt particles small coded grey dots. People are never drawn: no body outline; urine appears only in sample cups; the brain and kidney are organ plates. At most three bright text items at once; earlier labels dim to grey.
